title: Marius, While Seeking a Girl in a Bonnet, Encounters a Man in a Cap
summary: Through autumn and winter Marius searches Paris in vain for the girl of the Luxembourg and sinks into melancholy. One day near the Invalides he glimpses a white-haired workingman who looks like M. Leblanc, but loses him in the side streets.
details: Summer, autumn and winter pass, and neither M. Leblanc nor the girl returns to the Luxembourg. Marius has one thought left: to see her face again. He looks everywhere and finds nothing. The hopeful, planning young man becomes, in the narrator's phrase, a lost dog. Work disgusts him; he reproaches himself endlessly for having followed her and spoiled everything. Courfeyrac, who is told nothing and guesses a good deal, first congratulates him on being in love and then, seeing the gloom, tells him he has been an animal and drags him off to the Chaumière.

Once, trusting a fine September sun, Marius lets Courfeyrac, Bossuet and Grantaire take him to the ball at Sceaux in the wild hope of finding her there. He does not, and walks home alone through the night past the carts of singing revellers, while Grantaire grumbles that this is where all lost women turn up. Marius grows more and more solitary, going and coming in his pain like a wolf in a trap.

On another day, in the narrow streets near the Boulevard des Invalides, he passes a man dressed as a workingman, in a long-visored cap that shows locks of very white hair. The man walks slowly, as if absorbed in painful thought, and Marius believes he recognises M. Leblanc: the same hair, the same profile, the same bearing, only sadder. Why the workman's clothes? By the time Marius decides to follow, the man has turned into some side street and is gone. The encounter occupies him for three days and then fades; he tells himself it was probably only a resemblance.

title: Treasure Trove
summary: On Candlemas evening Marius, now almost the only lodger left in the Gorbeau house besides the Jondrettes, is jostled on the boulevard by two ragged girls fleeing the police. They drop a small grey packet of papers, which he picks up and pockets.
details: Marius still lives in the Gorbeau house and pays no attention to anyone in it. By now the only other inhabitants are the Jondrettes, the family whose rent he once paid without ever speaking to them; the rest have moved away, died or been turned out. It is the 2nd of February, Candlemas, with a treacherous bit of afternoon sun that the almanac-makers say heralds six weeks of cold. Marius leaves his room at nightfall to go and dine, passing Ma'am Bougon sweeping and lamenting that nothing in the world is cheap except trouble.

Walking up the boulevard towards the Rue Saint-Jacques with his head down, he is elbowed in the dusk by two girls in rags, one tall and slim, the other a little shorter, running breathless and terrified. The taller mutters in slang that the police nearly caught her at the half-circle; the other answers that she bolted. They vanish among the trees. Marius then notices a little greyish packet at his feet, an envelope that seems to hold papers. He assumes the girls dropped it, calls after them without result, and puts it in his pocket.

On the way to dinner he passes a child's coffin on three chairs in an alley of the Rue Mouffetard, and thinks of the two girls: sadder than seeing one's children die is seeing them lead an evil life. Then the shadows pass and he returns to his habitual thoughts of his six months of happiness under the trees of the Luxembourg. Young girls still appear to him, he reflects, but where they used to be angels, now they are ghouls.

title: Quadrifrons
summary: That night Marius opens the packet and finds four begging letters to four different patrons, signed with four different names but all plainly written by the same hand on the same tobacco-scented paper. Next morning a soft knock brings a young girl to his door.
details: Undressing for bed, Marius finds the forgotten packet in his coat and opens it, hoping it will tell him where to return it. Inside are four unsealed letters, all reeking of tobacco. One, to a Marquise de Grucheray, is from "Don Alvarès", a Spanish royalist cavalry captain stranded in France. One, to a Comtesse de Montvernet, is from "Mistress Balizard", an abandoned mother of six. One, to a stocking merchant named Pabourgeot, is from "Genflot, man of letters", who has sent a drama to the Théâtre-Français and will accept as little as forty sous. The fourth, to "the benevolent gentleman of the church of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas", is from "P. Fabantou, dramatic artist", who promises to show his certificates if the gentleman will follow his daughter home.

None gives an address, and though they claim four writers, all four are in the same handwriting, on the same coarse yellow paper, with the same spelling mistakes reproduced with great tranquillity. Marius concludes they come from one person, finds the petty mystery not worth solving, and tosses the envelope into a corner. Nothing proves it even belonged to the two girls.

About seven the next morning, as he settles to work, there is a gentle knock. Marius, who never locks his door since he owns nothing worth stealing (Ma'am Bougon once triumphed when a pair of old boots went missing), calls "Come in" without looking up, assuming it is she. A hoarse, broken voice, roughened with drink and sounding like an old man's, says "Excuse me, sir". He turns and sees a young girl.

title: A Rose in Misery
summary: The visitor is the elder Jondrette girl, ragged and half-starved, bringing a begging letter from her father in the same hand as the four Marius found. She roams his room, boasts that she can read and write, flirts clumsily, and leaves with the four letters and Marius's last five francs.
details: In the half-open door stands a girl of about sixteen in nothing but a chemise and petticoat, barefoot, emaciated, with missing teeth and bold dull eyes: a face that must once have been pretty and now shows fifty years mixed with fifteen. She knows his name, calls him Monsieur Marius, and hands him a letter whose wafer is still moist. It is from his neighbour Jondrette: the family has had no bread for two days, four persons and a sick wife, and he hopes the young man who paid his rent six months ago will help again. The writing, spelling, paper and tobacco smell are those of the four letters. Don Alvarès, Mistress Balizard, Genflot and Fabantou are all Jondrette, if Jondrette is really his name.

Marius now understands his neighbour's trade: writing under false names to people he thinks rich and charitable, and sending his daughters out to deliver the letters at their own peril. The two girls he jostled on the boulevard were these two; he had never really looked at them. While he reflects, the girl wanders the garret with the boldness of a ghost, rummaging, handling his clothes, delighted to find a mirror. She seizes an open book and reads a line about the attack on Hougomont, declares that her father was at Waterloo and that they are good Bonapartists, then takes a pen and writes "The bobbies are here" to prove she can spell. "We have not always been as we are now," she begins, and breaks off with a laugh. She hums a street song about hunger and cold, chatters about the theatre and a little brother who gets her tickets, and tells Marius he is a handsome fellow and that she often sees him going to Father Mabeuf's.

Marius retreats and hands her the envelope of four letters. She is overjoyed: she and her sister had searched everywhere, and rather than be beaten had told their father the letters were delivered and refused. She picks out the one for "the old fellow who goes to mass" at Saint-Jacques and says she will carry it to him now; it is his hour. In a wandering monologue she describes sleeping under bridges last winter, thinking of drowning herself but finding the water too cold, and the hallucinations that come when one has not eaten.

Marius searches his pockets and finds five francs sixteen sous, all he owns. He keeps the sixteen sous and gives her the five francs. She erupts in slang about wine and meat and a royal feast, bows, snatches a mouldy crust from his commode and bites into it on her way out.

title: A Providential Peephole
summary: Shaken by his first sight of real misery, Marius reproaches himself for ignoring the family beyond his wall for so long. Examining the thin partition, he finds a triangular hole near the ceiling and climbs onto his commode to look into the Jondrettes' garret.
details: Marius has known five years of poverty, but he realises he has never seen true misery until this girl passed before him. The narrator reflects that a man at his last extremity drags the weak around him, women and children, down with him into shame, and that despair is walled in by fragile partitions that open on vice or crime. The girl was a messenger from that realm of shadows.

Marius blames himself. Only a wall separated him from these abandoned beings; he heard them live and groan beside him every day and never listened, his mind given up to dreams and loves in the air. A less dreamy, more attentive neighbour would have noticed their distress and had them rescued. However corrupt and vile they seem, few fall without being degraded, and there is a point where the unfortunate and the infamous meet in one word, "the miserable"; charity should be deeper the deeper the fall.

Staring at the wall as if his pity could warm the people behind it, he studies its bare laths and plaster and suddenly notices, near the ceiling, a triangular gap between three laths where the plaster is missing. From the top of his commode one can see into the Jondrettes' attic. Commiseration, the narrator says, has its curiosity: one may look at misfortune like a traitor in order to help it. Marius climbs up and puts his eye to the hole.

title: The Wild Man in His Lair
summary: Through the hole Marius sees the Jondrettes' filthy, cavernous garret: the father, a small grey-bearded man in a woman's chemise, writing more begging letters and cursing the rich; the huge wife crouched by a dying fire; and the younger daughter sitting half-naked on a pallet, apparently neither seeing nor hearing.
details: Cities, like forests, have caverns where their most wicked creatures hide, but the city's are mean and ugly where the forest's are grand. What Marius sees is a hovel: a straw chair, a rickety table, broken crockery, two indescribable pallets, and a four-paned dormer draped in cobwebs. The walls are leprous and damp, scrawled with obscene charcoal drawings; the floor is bare blackened plaster. The one fireplace, which lets the room for forty francs a year, holds a brazier, a pot, boards, rags, a birdcage, ashes and two smouldering brands. The garret is large, full of black nooks. On the wall hangs a coloured print called The Dream, with Napoleon on a column lettered with misspelt battle names; beneath it a wooden panel leans with its face to the wall.

At the table sits a man of about sixty, small, thin, livid, with a cunning, cruel, uneasy look, a long grey beard, and a woman's chemise over muddy trousers and burst boots. He smokes a pipe (there is no bread, but there is tobacco) and writes, probably more letters like the four. A tattered novel of 1814 lies on the table. He talks aloud as he writes, raging that even in death there is no equality, since the rich lie up on the paved alley of Père-Lachaise and the poor are put in the mud below to rot faster. He strikes the table: he could eat the whole world.

A big woman of forty or a hundred squats on bare heels by the fire, in chemise and patched petticoat, with reddish-blond hair going grey and huge shining hands; a giant beside her husband, with another volume of the same romance open on the floor. On one pallet sits a tall, pale, half-naked girl with dangling feet who seems not to listen, see or live: the younger sister, who looks eleven or twelve and is really fourteen, the one who said "I bolted" on the boulevard. There is no sign of work anywhere, only some dubious ironmongery in a corner.

The man goes on grumbling that everybody is canaille. The woman, with the flattened affection of long misery, tells her "little friend" to calm himself; he is too good to write to all those people. He keeps writing.

title: Strategy and Tactics
summary: The elder girl bursts in: the gentleman from Saint-Jacques has read the letter and is coming in a cab with his daughter. Jondrette hastily stages their misery, dousing the fire, kicking the seat out of the chair, making the younger girl break a windowpane (she cuts her hand), and ordering his wife to bed.
details: As Marius is about to climb down, the door of the garret flies open and the elder girl appears in men's shoes caked with mud and a tattered mantle, breathless and triumphant: "He is coming!" The philanthropist from the church of Saint-Jacques read the letter, asked her address, said his daughter had purchases to make and that he would take a carriage and arrive as soon as she did. He seemed surprised and hesitated when she named the house, then said never mind. She saw the father and daughter get into a fiacre after mass, and has just seen it turn into the Rue Petit-Banquier; she even noted its number, 440. "He is Rothschild," says her father, and praises her as a clever girl. She retorts that she will not wear these squelching shoes again; he answers that the poor must have shoes to enter churches, one cannot go barefoot to God.

Then he springs into action like a general before battle. He tells his wife to put out the fire, and when she does not move, douses the brands himself with a jug of water. He kicks his leg through the straw seat of the only chair. Learning it is snowing, he orders the younger girl off the bed to break a pane; the bewildered child obeys with her fist and the glass clatters down. He orders his wife into bed, and she obeys. A sob comes from the corner: the little girl has cut her wrist. The mother protests; the father says so much the better, he foresaw it, and tears a strip from the chemise he is wearing to bind the wound, pleased that the torn chemise too looks well.

Icy wind and mist pour through the broken pane; the snow promised by the Candlemas sun has come. Jondrette spreads ashes over the wet brands to hide them, surveys the room, and leans against the chimney-piece: now they can receive the philanthropist.

title: The Ray of Light in the Hovel
summary: While the family waits in the cold, Jondrette rants against charitable rich men who bring old clothes instead of money. Then the visitors arrive, and Marius, watching through the hole, sees that the young lady is the girl of the Luxembourg, accompanied by M. Leblanc.
details: The elder girl puts her cold hand in her father's; he says he is colder still, and when his wife remarks that he always has something better than everyone else, even bad things, he silences her with a look. The mother kisses and soothes the sobbing younger child; the father tells her to keep sobbing, that's right. He frets that the man may not come after all, and that he will have put out his fire, wrecked his chair, torn his shirt and broken his pane for nothing; "and wounded the child," the mother murmurs.

He works himself into a fury against the rich who go to mass, give to priests, and come to humiliate the poor with old duds not worth four sous and bread, when what he wants is money, which they refuse because they say the poor would drink it. They are thieves themselves, he says; society ought to be grasped by the four corners and tossed into the air so that no one has anything.

A light tap at the door. Jondrette rushes to open it, bowing and smiling, and bids the respected benefactor and his charming young lady enter. A man of ripe age and a young girl step onto the threshold. Marius, at his post, is overwhelmed: it is She, the face he has sought for six months, a little pale, in a violet velvet bonnet and black satin pelisse, reappearing in this horror. She is still accompanied by M. Leblanc. She sets a bulky parcel on the table. Behind the door the elder Jondrette girl stares with sombre eyes at the velvet bonnet, the silk mantle and the happy face.

title: Jondrette Comes Near Weeping
summary: Jondrette, remembering just in time that he signed himself Fabantou, plays the ruined actor for M. Leblanc, lying that he owes sixty francs by that evening. Leblanc gives five francs, leaves his greatcoat, and promises to return at six with the sixty francs; meanwhile Jondrette twice tells his wife to take a good look at the man.
details: Coming from daylight, the visitors can barely see in the dark den while its inhabitants see them clearly. M. Leblanc, with his sad kindly look, presents the package of new clothes, woollen stockings and blankets. Jondrette bows to the ground, then whispers to his daughter, "Duds, no money, they are all alike," and asks how the letter was signed. "Fabantou," she says, just as Leblanc gropes for the name. Jondrette supplies it and launches into his act: a pupil of Talma, once favoured by fortune, now without bread or fire, his chair seatless, his pane broken, his wife ill in bed, his child wounded. He pinches the little girl's sore hand to make her shriek, and the young lady hurries to comfort her. The wrist, he says, was hurt at a machine earning six sous a day and the arm may have to come off.

All the while he studies the benefactor strangely, as if trying to remember something. Passing his wife's bed, he whispers, "Take a look at that man!" Then he resumes his lamentations: his only garment is his wife's chemise; if he had a coat he would go to see Mademoiselle Mars, who played with him in the provinces; his wife has suffocating fits; he has brought up his daughters religiously and kept them from the stage. And tomorrow, the fourth of February, is his landlord's last day of grace: if the rent is not paid tonight, all four will be turned into the snow. He owes four quarters, sixty francs. The narrator notes the lie: four quarters would be forty, and he cannot owe four since Marius paid two less than six months ago.

M. Leblanc tosses five francs on the table (Jondrette mutters that it will not even pay for his chair and pane), takes off his big brown greatcoat and lays it over the chair, and says these five francs are all he has with him; he will take his daughter home and return this evening, when the rent is due. Jondrette's face lights up strangely. Six o'clock, says Leblanc, with the sixty francs. "Take a good look at him, wife!" Jondrette whispers again. As the visitors turn to go, the elder girl points out the forgotten coat and gets an annihilating look from her father; Leblanc smiles that he is leaving it, and tells Jondrette to put it on if he comes out, since it is very cold. Jondrette dons it and sees them down to their carriage.

title: Tariff of Licensed Cabs: Two Francs an Hour
summary: Marius rushes down to follow the fiacre but, with only sixteen sous left after his gift to the girl, cannot pay a cab in advance and loses it. Returning in despair, he sees Jondrette in the greatcoat talking on the boulevard with a prowler who resembles Panchaud, alias Bigrenaille.
details: Marius has seen the whole scene and yet seen nothing but her. He watched her unpack the clothes and question the mother and the hurt child kindly, straining to hear her voice, which he has never clearly heard, but Jondrette's trumpeting drowned everything. A hummingbird among toads, he thinks. When she leaves he has one idea: to follow and learn where she lives. He hesitates, fearing that if M. Leblanc catches sight of him on the stairs he will take alarm and vanish for good, then risks it. The corridor and stairs are empty, and from the boulevard he sees the fiacre turning into the Rue du Petit-Banquier, then far down the Rue Mouffetard.

An empty cab passes. Marius hails it: "By the hour?" The driver eyes the young man with no cravat, a buttonless working-coat and a torn shirt, and rubs his thumb and finger: pay in advance, forty sous. Marius has sixteen. "I will pay on my return." The driver whistles and whips up his horse. For want of twenty-four sous Marius has lost his joy; he reflects bitterly on the five francs he gave the wretched girl that morning. He does not seem to register that Leblanc has promised to come back at six.

About to climb the stairs, he notices across the boulevard, by the deserted wall of the Rue de la Barrière-des-Gobelins, Jondrette in the philanthropist's greatcoat deep in talk with one of the "prowlers of the barriers", men of suspicious face who sleep by day. Marius barely attends, yet thinks the man resembles a certain Panchaud, alias Printanier, alias Bigrenaille, whom Courfeyrac once pointed out as a very dangerous night roamer. The narrator adds that this Panchaud, already watched by the police in 1832, went on to figure in many criminal trials and carved his name in a sewer of La Force during an escape attempt.

title: Offers of Service from Misery to Wretchedness
summary: The elder Jondrette girl follows Marius to his door, notices his sadness and offers to help him in anything. He asks her to find the address of the old gentleman and his daughter; she agrees, bitterly aware it is the daughter he wants, and he promises her anything she likes. Then he hears Jondrette declare that he has recognised the visitor.
details: Climbing the stairs, Marius finds the elder Jondrette girl following him. He finds the sight of her odious: she has his five francs, and it is useless to ask her where the visitors live since the letter was addressed only to "the benevolent gentleman of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas". He pushes his door, but her hand holds it open. She has lost her morning's assurance and does not look at him. "Monsieur Marius, you look sad. What is the matter with you?" He denies it and tells her to leave him alone; she holds on. He was kind this morning, she says; let him be kind again and tell her what ails him. She can be useful: she carries letters, goes from door to door, finds addresses, follows people, for her father.

An idea strikes Marius; what branch does a falling man disdain? He draws near and says "Listen", and she begs him to call her "thou". She brought the old gentleman and his daughter here; does she know their address? No. "Find it for me." Her joyful eyes go dark. Does he know them? No. "That is to say, you do not know her, but you wish to know her." She promises him "the beautiful lady's" address, a phrase that troubles him so that he adds, never mind, the address of father and daughter. "What will you give me?" "Anything you like." She drops her head and pulls the door shut behind her.

Marius sinks into a chair, dizzy with the day: the angel's appearance and disappearance, this creature's offer, a gleam of hope in a vast despair. Then Jondrette's shrill voice through the wall rouses him: "I tell you that I am sure of it, and that I recognized him." Whom? M. Leblanc? Does Jondrette know him? Is Marius about to learn at last who it is that he loves and who her father is? He bounds onto the commode and puts his eye to the hole.

title: The Use Made of M. Leblanc’s Five-Franc Piece
summary: Marius overhears Jondrette tell his wife that he recognised their visitor from eight years ago, whisper a name about the young lady that fills her with rage, and announce that his fortune is made: the "Croesus" will return at six, when the house is empty, and if he does not give in, "we'll fix him". Jondrette goes out to see some people, leaving orders for a charcoal brazier.
details: The wife and daughters have put on the new stockings and jackets and the blankets lie on the beds. Jondrette has just come in from outside and paces with extraordinary eyes. "Sure! Eight years have passed! But I recognize him!" Only older, better dressed, the same voice. He sends the girls out, keeping the elder back to order both of them to be there at five o'clock precisely; he will need them. Alone with his wife, he says: "The young lady—" and whispers in her ear, then concludes aloud, "It is she!" The mother's fury is monstrous: it cannot be, when her own daughters go barefoot; a satin pelisse, a velvet bonnet, two hundred francs of clothes; the other one was hideous and this one is not bad-looking. "That horrible, beautiful young lady, who gazed at my daughters with an air of pity—she is that beggar brat!" She would like to kick her stomach in. Marius finds her more frightening than her husband.

Then Jondrette announces, "My fortune is made." He has had enough of misery; he wants to eat and drink and sleep and be a bit of a millionaire, like other people. Lowering his voice (but not enough, and the snow deadens the traffic outside), he explains: the Croesus is as good as caught. He has seen some people; everything is arranged. The man will come at six to bring sixty francs, fooled by the tale of the landlord and the fourth of February; six is when the neighbour dines, Mother Bougon is out washing dishes in town, and the neighbour never returns before eleven. The children will stand watch, the wife will help. "He will give in." And if not? A sinister gesture: "We'll fix him," and a cold, sweet laugh that makes Marius shudder.

He puts on an old cap to go and see "some more people, good ones", congratulates himself that the man did not recognise him in return, thanks to his romantic beard, and that the greatcoat lets him go out at all. He comes back to add that a brazier of charcoal, two good bushels, must be ready, and throws his wife the five-franc piece, warning her not to spend it all: he needs about three francs for something at the ironmonger's in the Rue Mouffetard. Eating is not the point today. As his step dies away on the stairs, one o'clock strikes from Saint-Médard.

title: Solus Cum Solo, in Loco Remoto, Non Cogitabuntur Orare Pater Noster
summary: Resolved to crush the trap, Marius slips out to find the police. Passing a low wall in the Rue du Petit-Banquier he overhears two men sitting in the snow discussing an "affair" that cannot fail with Patron-Minette's help, and reflects that losing his five francs that morning is what let him discover the plot.
details: Marius, kindly as a brahmin and severe as a judge, pities a toad but crushes a viper, and he has just looked into a nest of vipers. None of his enigmas is solved; he knows only that Jondrette is acquainted with M. Leblanc and the girl, that an ambush is being prepared, and that both are in danger, the father certainly, the daughter probably. They must be saved. He feels a secret joy at the chance of serving the one he loves. But how to warn them? He has no address. Waiting at the door at six would only get him seized by Jondrette's men and doom the victim. It is one o'clock; he has five hours. He puts on his decent coat and a silk handkerchief and creeps out while the Jondrette woman rummages in her heap of old iron.

Halfway along the Rue du Petit-Banquier, by a low wall bordering waste ground, he hears voices in the empty street. Looking over the wall he sees two strangers sitting in the snow with their backs to it: a bearded man in a blouse and fez, and a long-haired, bareheaded man in rags with snow in his hair. The long-haired one says that with Patron-Minette's help it cannot fail; it is worth five hundred francs a head and at worst five, six, ten years; "Father What's-his-name's" team will already be harnessed. The bearded one shivers and agrees you cannot go against such things. Then they discuss a melodrama they saw at the Gaîté. Marius walks on, sure this must be "the affair".

He asks at a shop in the Faubourg Saint-Marceau for the commissary of police and is directed to No. 14, Rue de Pontoise. On the way he buys a two-sou roll, knowing he will not dine, and gives Providence its due: had he not given his five francs to the Jondrette girl, he would have followed the fiacre, known nothing, and M. Leblanc and his daughter would have walked into the trap.

title: In Which a Police Agent Bestows Two Fistfuls on a Lawyer
summary: At the police station Marius tells a tall, ferocious inspector about the trap. The inspector knows the Gorbeau house and the gang, takes Marius's passkey, gives him two loaded pistols, and tells him to watch through the hole and fire a shot into the air when the crime is about to be committed, not too soon. As Marius leaves, the man gives his name: Inspector Javert.
details: The commissary is absent; an inspector takes his place. Behind a grating stands a tall man in a vast three-collared topcoat, with a square face, thin mouth, grey whiskers and a look that turns your pockets inside out, no less terrible to meet than Jondrette: the dog, the narrator says, can be as alarming as the wolf. He asks "What do you want?" without a "monsieur". Marius, giving his name and calling himself a lawyer, tells everything: a person he knows only by sight is to be drawn into a trap that evening; he heard the plot through the partition of the neighbouring room; the planner is one Jondrette; accomplices will include prowlers of the barriers such as Panchaud, alias Bigrenaille; the daughters will keep watch; the victim's name is unknown; the hour is six, at No. 50–52 on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital.

At the number the inspector looks up: the room at the end of the corridor? Apparently he knows the house, the former property of Gorbeau. He mutters that Patron-Minette must have a hand in it, and when Marius repeats the talk behind the wall, identifies the long-haired man as Brujon and the bearded one as Demi-Liard, alias Deux-Milliards, and thinks he recognises "Father What's-his-name" too. He asks whether Marius saw a little dandy, a big lump like an elephant, a scamp like an old red-tail; as for the fourth, no one sees him. He will not say who they are. Hiding police inside the house would only make the "artists" call off the performance; he wants to hear them sing and make them dance.

"Are you afraid?" "No more than yourself!" Marius retorts, stung at still not being called monsieur. The inspector approves: courage does not fear crime, honesty does not fear authority. He asks for Marius's passkey to the house and pockets it, and when Marius advises him to come in force, pulls two small steel pistols from his pockets, "knock-me-downs", each with two balls. Marius is to go home, hide in his room as if out, watch through the hole, let the men proceed, and when the crime is about to be committed fire a shot into the ceiling; above all, not too soon. The rest concerns him. He makes Marius move the pistols to his trousers pockets, checks the time (half past two) and, as Marius reaches the door, adds that if he needs anything before then he should ask for Inspector Javert.

title: Jondrette Makes His Purchases
summary: Courfeyrac and Bossuet spot Marius in the snowy Rue Mouffetard shadowing Jondrette, who visits a hovel, buys a large cold chisel at an ironmonger's and climbs over the wall in the Rue du Petit-Banquier. Marius hurries home before Ma'am Bougon locks up and glimpses four motionless men in an empty attic along his corridor.
details: About three o'clock Courfeyrac and Bossuet, walking in the thickening snow ("a plague of white butterflies in heaven," says Bossuet), catch sight of Marius coming up the street with a peculiar air. Courfeyrac says not to speak to him: he is busy, following someone, in love. But there is no woman in the street; he is following a man in a grey cap and grey beard, wearing a brand-new greatcoat too large for him over frightful ragged trousers. "He's a poet," Courfeyrac decides, and refuses to follow a man who is following another man.

Marius has indeed seen Jondrette in the Rue Mouffetard and is spying on him. Jondrette enters one of the worst hovels of the Rue Gracieuse for a quarter of an hour, returns, stops at an ironmonger's at the corner of the Rue Pierre-Lombard and comes out with a huge white-handled cold chisel, which he hides under his coat, then hurries to the Rue du Petit-Banquier. Marius wisely waits at the corner: Jondrette looks round to make sure he is not followed, then springs over the low wall where Marius heard the two men talking. The waste ground beyond adjoins the back yard of a failed livery-stable keeper of bad repute who still keeps a few old carriages in his sheds.

Night is falling and a red moon rises behind the Salpêtrière. Marius has given his key to the inspector, and Ma'am Bougon locks the house at dusk when she goes to wash dishes in town, so he hurries back. The door is still open. Creeping along the corridor, where all the empty attics stand open, he thinks he sees in one of them the motionless heads of four men in the last of the daylight. He does not try to look, reaches his room unseen, and a moment later hears Ma'am Bougon leave and lock the house behind her.

title: In Which Will Be Found the Words to an English Air Which Was in Fashion in 1832
summary: Marius waits in his dark room as Jondrette returns and tells the family all is going well: "The mousetrap is open. The cats are there." Sent to check the neighbour's room, the elder girl finds Marius hidden under his bed but spends her time primping in his mirror and singing, then the two girls are posted outside as lookouts.
details: At half past five Marius sits on his bed hearing his own pulse, thinking of crime advancing on one side and justice on the other. The snow has stopped and moonlight gives the room a twilight glow; the hole in the wall shines with a reddish light that seems bloody, though the Jondrette den is utterly silent. He takes off his boots. Then the street door turns, a heavy step mounts, and Jondrette comes in to the yelps of his family. All is first-rate, he says, though his feet are frozen; he approves of their having dressed up, since they must inspire confidence. He lays something heavy on the table, probably the chisel. The mother has cooked three potatoes on the fire; tomorrow, he promises, they will dine like Charles the Tenth. "The mousetrap is open. The cats are there." He tells her to put something in the fire; Marius hears charcoal being handled. The hinges have been greased.

It is nearly six. Jondrette asks whether old Bougon has left and whether anyone is in the neighbour's room; the mother says he has been out all day and this is his dinner hour, but Jondrette sends the elder girl with a candle to make sure. Marius crawls under his bed. The girl reports from the door that the key is in the lock so he must be out; her father makes her go in anyway. She walks straight to the mirror nailed by the bed, smooths her hair, smiles at herself, and sings a sentimental song about a love that lasted a week, while iron is moved about next door. She looks out of the window ("How ugly Paris is when it has put on a white chemise!") and preens again, answering her father's shout that she is looking under the bed and furniture and there is no one. She sings another verse and leaves.

Marius hears the girls' bare feet in the corridor and Jondrette's orders: one at the barrier, one at the corner of the Rue du Petit-Banquier; watch the door and run up at the first sign of anything. The elder grumbles at standing watch barefoot in the snow; tomorrow, says her father, she shall have dainty green silk boots. The outer door bangs. Now only Marius, the Jondrettes and the mysterious men in the empty attic remain in the house.

title: The Use Made of Marius’ Five-Franc Piece
summary: Back at the peephole, Marius sees the garret lit by a brazier of glowing charcoal with the chisel heating in it, heaps of rope and iron by the door, and a rope ladder. Jondrette sends his wife down with a lantern to admit the visitor and dismiss his cab, and she takes Marius's two chairs from his room without seeing him in the dark. Jondrette tests a kitchen knife; Marius cocks his pistol.
details: The den is lit less by its candle than by the red glow of a large sheet-iron brazier in the fireplace, full of burning charcoal, with the chisel from the Rue Pierre-Lombard thrust in to heat; the heat makes the candle droop. By the door lie two heaps, one of old iron and one of rope. A copper dark-lantern stands on the chimney-piece. The brazier's fumes go up the chimney and the broken pane airs the room, so nothing betrays it. The narrator recalls that this is the most retired room in the most isolated house on the most deserted boulevard in Paris; its only window gives on walled waste ground. If ambushes had not existed, they would have been invented here.

Jondrette smokes on the seatless chair while his wife, absurd in a plumed black bonnet, an immense tartan shawl and the men's shoes her daughter scorned, talks low. Jondrette still wears M. Leblanc's too-large coat. He instructs her: the man will come in a carriage; she is to wait behind the street door with the lantern, open at once, light him up the stairs and corridor, then go down, pay the coachman and send the fiacre away. For the fare he hands her the five francs the neighbour gave them that morning. Then he says two chairs will be needed, "to sit on", a mild answer that chills Marius, and she goes to fetch the neighbour's. Marius has no time to hide. She enters by moonlight, which leaves the wall he leans on in deep shadow, takes his only two chairs, and leaves without seeing him.

Jondrette sets the chairs on either side of the table, turns the chisel in the brazier, masks the fire with an old screen, and bends over the rope pile, which Marius now sees is a well-made rope ladder with wooden rungs and two hooks. The heavy tools mixed with the old iron were not there in the morning; Marius takes them for an edge-tool maker's, though a more knowing eye would recognise burglars' instruments for forcing locks and cutting. The candle is now the only light. Jondrette, his pipe gone out, pulls open the table drawer, takes out a long kitchen knife, tries its edge on his nail and puts it back. Marius draws and cocks his pistol; at the click Jondrette starts and listens, then laughs that it is only the partition cracking. Marius keeps the pistol in his hand.

title: Marius’ Two Chairs Form a Vis-a-Vis
summary: Six strikes from Saint-Médard and M. Leblanc arrives, serene, laying four louis on the table for the rent. His cab is dismissed, he and Jondrette sit facing each other across the table, and Marius watches from behind the wall, pistol in hand, sure that the police are waiting for his signal.
details: The clock of Saint-Médard strikes six; Jondrette nods at each stroke, snuffs the candle with his fingers, paces, and listens at the corridor, muttering "Provided only that he comes!" The door opens: his wife stands in the corridor with the dark-lantern lighting her grimace from below. "Enter, sir." M. Leblanc appears, with an air of serenity that makes him singularly venerable, and lays four louis on the table for Monsieur Fabantou's rent and most pressing needs; the rest, he says, they will attend to hereafter. Jondrette whispers to his wife to dismiss the carriage; she slips out and returns: it is done. The snow is so deep that the fiacre's coming and going are inaudible.

Leblanc takes one chair, Jondrette the other, facing him. The narrator asks the reader to picture the scene: a cold night, the snowbound solitudes of the Salpêtrière white as shrouds in the moonlight, the red street lanterns and black elms of the deserted boulevard, the Gorbeau hovel at its pitch of silence and darkness, and in it the vast garret lit by a single candle, two men at a table, Leblanc tranquil, Jondrette smiling and alarming, the she-wolf in a corner, and behind the partition Marius, erect and invisible, missing nothing, pistol in hand.

Marius feels horror but no fear. He grips the pistol: he can stop that wretch whenever he pleases. He is sure the police are somewhere in ambush waiting for the agreed signal, and he hopes this encounter will throw light on everything he longs to know.

title: Occupying One’s Self with Obscure Depths
summary: Jondrette keeps up his patter about his poverty and a "picture by a master" he must sell, while four men with blackened faces slip silently into the room and sit on the bed behind him. When Leblanc values the daub at three francs, Jondrette asks a thousand crowns, then suddenly drops the mask and thunders: "Do you know me?"
details: M. Leblanc asks after the wounded little girl; her sister, says Jondrette, has taken her to the Bourbe hospital and they will be back shortly. The wife, in her eccentric finery, has placed herself between him and the door in an attitude of menace. When Leblanc remarks that Madame Fabantou seems better, Jondrette says she is dying but has the courage of an ox; flattered, she calls him Monsieur Jondrette, and he hastily explains the slip as an artistic sobriquet, Fabantou alias Jondrette. He rambles on about their happy marriage, their willingness to work, his wish to have his girls taught paper-box making, and the one relic of his prosperity, a picture he is willing to sell.

Marius notices a man who has entered without a sound and sat on the nearest bed behind Jondrette: in a ragged knitted vest, wooden shoes, no shirt, bare tattooed arms, and a face smeared with black. Leblanc turns at the same moment and cannot hide his surprise. Jondrette pretends to think he is admiring the coat, then calls the man a neighbour not worth attention. A second blackened man glides in and sits beside the first. Jondrette says they belong in the house and turns the panel against the wall round: a coarse daub with a central figure in crude colours, which he calls a painting by a master, as dear to him as his two daughters.

Leblanc's eye returns to the back of the room, where there are now four men, three on the bed and one by the doorpost, all bare-armed, motionless and black-faced; one, old, with white hair, leans against the wall with closed eyes as if asleep, and of the two younger one is bearded and the other long-haired. Jondrette calls them friends and neighbours, chimney-builders black from charcoal, and presses him to buy. Looking him full in the eye, Leblanc says it is some tavern signboard worth about three francs. Jondrette sweetly asks whether he has his pocketbook: he would be satisfied with a thousand crowns. Leblanc springs up with his back to the wall, Jondrette on his left by the window, the woman and the four men on his right by the door.

Jondrette resumes his whine about the paper-box trade, four sous a day for fourteen hours' work, and his thoughts of drowning himself from the steps by the bridge of Austerlitz, his eye all the while on the door, so that Leblanc seems to wonder whether the man has gone mad. Then his dull eyes flash, he draws himself up and takes a step towards Leblanc, crying in a voice of thunder that none of this is the point: "Do you know me?"

title: The Trap
summary: Three masked men join the ambush and Jondrette declares himself to be Thénardier, the innkeeper of Montfermeil, accusing M. Leblanc of being the man who took the Lark from him eight years ago; Leblanc denies knowing him. Marius, hearing the name his father's will commanded him to honour, cannot bring himself to fire. Leblanc is overpowered and bound, forced to write a note to his daughter, and gives a false address; when the ruse is discovered he frees himself and burns his own arm with the red-hot chisel to show he cannot be made to speak. As Thénardier advances with his knife, Marius tosses in the girl's note "The bobbies are here", and the gang is scrambling for the rope ladder when Javert appears in the doorway.
details: Three men in blue blouses and black paper masks enter: a thin one with an iron-tipped cudgel, a colossus with a butcher's poleaxe, and a thickset man with an enormous prison key. Jondrette checks with the thin man that all is ready, that the carriage with two good horses is waiting where ordered, and that Montparnasse has stopped to chat with his eldest girl. M. Leblanc, very pale but without fear, has made a rampart of the table and suddenly looks less like a kindly old man than an athlete. Marius feels proud of the unknown man and raises his pistol towards the ceiling. Three of the "chimney-builders" arm themselves with shears, tongs and a hammer and block the door. Jondrette repeats his question, leans across the candle, and says: his name is not Fabantou, nor Jondrette, but Thénardier, the innkeeper of Montfermeil. Leblanc replies with perfect calm that he knows him no more than before.

Marius does not hear the answer. The name Thénardier is the one written in his father's will, "a certain Thénardier saved my life; if my son encounters him, he will do him all the good that lies in his power": the name he has carried for four years and sought in vain. His father's saviour is a ruffian about to commit something like murder, and against the father of the girl he loves. If he fires, Leblanc is saved and Thénardier lost; if not, Leblanc is sacrificed. Remorse waits either way; his knees give way. Thénardier, whom the narrator says he will henceforth call by no other name, paces in wild triumph and pours out his grievance: it was Leblanc who came to his inn on Christmas eve 1823 in a yellow greatcoat, carried off "that Fantine's child", the Lark, for fifteen hundred francs, a girl who belonged to rich people and would have kept him all his life, and who threatened him with a cudgel in the woods; now Thénardier holds the trumps. He laughs at how easily his tale of the landlord and the fourth of February was swallowed. Leblanc answers quietly that he is mistaken for someone else, a very poor man, not a millionaire. When Thénardier presses, Leblanc says politely: "I see that you are a villain!" Thénardier rages that the rich warm their feet and eat asparagus in January while the poor are the thermometers of the cold; he has been a licensed tradesman and an elector, an old soldier who at Waterloo saved a general whose name he never caught, only "Merci"; the picture, he says, painted by David, shows him carrying that general through the grapeshot. He wants money, a great deal of money. Marius, listening, has no doubt left: this is the Thénardier of the will, and the daub is the sign of the Montfermeil tavern, a battle, smoke, one man carrying another. His father seems to rise from the panel and look at him.

The man with the axe pulls off his mask for fun and cracks a joke from the corridor; while Thénardier scolds him with his back turned, Leblanc kicks over the chair and table and is half out of the window before six fists drag him back and the Thénardier woman winds her hands in his hair. The other ruffians rush in; the old drunk on the bed reels up with a stone-breaker's hammer. One blackened face Marius recognises as Panchaud, alias Bigrenaille, who raises a leaded bludgeon over Leblanc's head. Marius thinks "My father, forgive me!" and his finger finds the trigger, but Thénardier shouts "Don't harm him!" and the moment passes; the adroit man in him has replaced the ferocious one. Leblanc fells the old man, throws off two assailants and pins them under his knees, but four others hold him and he vanishes under the pile like a boar under hounds. They throw him on the bed by the window and search him: a purse with six francs and a handkerchief, no pocketbook, no watch. Thénardier pockets the handkerchief, has him tied upright to the leg of the bed, orders the drunk, whom he calls Boulatruelle, swept into a corner, and reproaches Babet, the man with the cudgel, for bringing so many; they all wanted to be in it, says Babet, business is slow.

Thénardier's face turns from violence to polished sweetness, a tiger become a lawyer. He points out that the prisoner has not cried out once, even while struggling: a man who does not want the police must have something to hide, as they do, so they can come to an understanding. He unmasks the brazier so the white-hot chisel can be seen, and names his price, two hundred thousand francs, not to be paid now, only to be written for. He has Bigrenaille untie the right arm and dictates a letter: "My dear daughter, come immediately, I am in absolute need of thee...", striking out "come with confidence" as likely to arouse distrust. Does he address "the little one, the Lark" as thou? Leblanc says he does not know what he means. Thénardier carefully avoids naming the girl before his accomplices. Asked his name, the prisoner says Urbain Fabre; the handkerchief is marked U. F. He addresses the letter to Mademoiselle Fabre, at M. Urbain Fabre's, No. 17 Rue Saint-Dominique-d'Enfer. Thénardier sends his wife off in the carriage with the letter and the axe-man riding behind, shouting after her not to lose the two hundred thousand francs she carries. He then explains the plan to "Monsieur Fabre": his wife, dressed to inspire confidence, will fetch the young lady; outside the barrier a trap with two good horses waits; his comrade will carry her to a quiet place and return her when the money is paid, and if Thénardier is arrested, the comrade will "give a turn of his thumb to the Lark". Marius, who now sees that the two letters meant Urbain Fabre and that "Ursule" was never her name, is held fast by the threat as much as by the will.

After half an hour the wife bursts in: false address, nobody at No. 17 but a carriage gate, no Monsieur Fabre; the old fellow has duped him, and she would have chopped the beast in quarters. Marius breathes: the girl is safe. "A false address? What did you expect to gain by that?" "To gain time!" cries the prisoner, shaking off his cut bonds; he is held only by one leg. He snatches the glowing chisel from the brazier and holds the gang at bay. The narrator explains that the later investigation found under the bed a hollowed sou piece of the kind made in the galleys, with a watch-spring saw inside, which he must have hidden in his hand when searched and used to cut his ropes. Declaring that his life is not worth defending and that they cannot make him write or speak what he does not choose, he bares his left arm and lays the red-hot iron on his own flesh; the room fills with the smell of burning, the ruffians shudder, and his face shows no hatred, only serene majesty. "Have no more fear of me than I have for you!" He hurls the chisel out of the window into the snow, says they may do what they please with him, and is seized again. Below the hole Marius hears husband and wife agree in a whisper to cut his throat. Thénardier takes the knife from the drawer. Marius, torn for an hour between his father's testament and the cry to save the prisoner, sees in a shaft of moonlight on his table the sheet on which the elder girl wrote that morning, "The bobbies are here", wraps it round a bit of plaster and tosses it through the hole into the den. The woman picks it up; Thénardier reads it and recognises Éponine's hand, concludes that since "Ponine" threw it through the window that side is not watched, and orders the ladder: leave the bacon in the mousetrap and decamp, no time to cut the man's throat. The ventriloquist-voiced man gives a silent signal, the ladder is hooked to the sill, and Thénardier rushes to go first, but Bigrenaille hauls him back by the collar, the ruffians insist on drawing lots, and Thénardier is shouting that they are mad, with names in a hat, when a voice from the threshold offers its hat. It is Javert, holding it out with a smile.

title: One Should Always Begin by Arresting the Victims
summary: Javert, who had already caught Azelma on watch outside and lost Éponine, arrests the whole gang after Thénardier's pistol misfires in his face and the Thénardier woman hurls a paving-stone at him. He greets each ruffian by name, then calls for the bound gentleman to come forward and finds that the victim has escaped out of the window.
details: The narrator backtracks: at nightfall Javert posted his men among the trees across the boulevard and began by pocketing the two girls set to watch the approaches, but he caged only Azelma; Éponine was not at her post and could not be found. Agitated by the comings and goings of fiacres and having recognised many of the ruffians who entered, he grew impatient and went up with Marius's passkey without waiting for the pistol shot, arriving in the nick of time.

The seven men snatch up their weapons; Thénardier grips his knife and the Thénardier woman a huge paving-stone that served her daughters as a stool. Javert, hat on, arms folded, cane under his arm, tells them they will go out by the door, not the window: there are seven of them and fifteen of him, no need to collar one another like men of Auvergne. Bigrenaille slips a pistol to Thénardier, not daring to fire at Javert himself; Thénardier aims at three paces, Javert tells him calmly that it will miss fire, and it does. Bigrenaille throws down his bludgeon and surrenders, asking only not to be denied tobacco in prison; the rest follow. Javert calls in his squad with swords and bludgeons. The Thénardier woman, shielding her husband behind her discarded shawl, raises the stone like a giantess and roars at the police to keep off; Javert advances, remarking that she has a beard like a man and he has claws like a woman, ducks the stone, and lays one hand on her shoulder and the other on her husband's head. Handcuffed, she weeps for her daughters. "They are in the jug," says Javert. The drunk wakes asking Jondrette whether it is all over; Javert answers yes.

Telling the masked men to keep their masks on, Javert reviews them like Frederick II at a parade: good day Bigrenaille, Brujon, Deuxmilliards, to the three chimney-builders; good day Gueulemer to the man with the axe, Babet to the man with the cudgel, and "your health, Claquesous" to the ventriloquist. He orders the gentleman untied and no one let out, sits down at the table to write his report, and after the first formulas asks the gentleman the others bound to step forward. He is gone. The door was guarded but the window was not; while the police were busy he slipped down the rope ladder, which is still swaying. "The devil!" mutters Javert; he must have been the most valuable of the lot.

title: The Little One Who Was Crying in Volume Two
summary: The next night a ragged, singing gamin kicks at the locked door of the Gorbeau house to visit "his ancestors". Ma'am Bougon tells him his father is at La Force, his mother at Saint-Lazare and his sisters at the Madelonettes; he says "Ah!", pirouettes and goes off singing.
details: On the evening after the ambush a pale, thin boy in rags and linen trousers comes singing up the boulevard from the direction of the bridge of Austerlitz. At the corner of the Rue du Petit-Banquier he jostles a bent old woman picking over a heap of refuse by a street lamp and mocks her for an enormous dog; she straightens in fury, her wrinkled face lit red by the lantern, and he tells her that madame does not possess the style of beauty which pleases him.

He reaches No. 50–52, finds the door locked, and batters it with heroic kicks that betray the man's shoes he is wearing rather than the child's feet inside them. The old woman hurries after him shrieking that he is knocking the house down, then recognises him: it is that imp. He greets her as Bougonmuche and says he has come to see his ancestors. There is no one here, she says. Where is his father? At La Force. His mother? At Saint-Lazare. His sisters? At the Madelonettes.

The boy scratches his head, says "Ah!", spins on his heel, and a moment later Ma'am Bougon hears his clear young voice singing his song about King Coupdesabot hunting crows on stilts as he plunges off under the black elms in the winter wind.

title: Well Cut
summary: Hugo opens Volume IV with history: how the Restoration, misreading its 1814 charter as a gift it could revoke, challenged the nation's sovereignty with the July ordinances and fell in 1830, and why the Revolution of July, as right overthrowing fact, was both formidable and gentle.
details: The narrator sets 1831 and 1832 apart as two mountain years of revolutionary grandeur and says he will try to grasp their principal lines. After the Empire, a weary nation wanted only rest; at the same time the accomplished facts of revolution and war demanded guarantees, as England demanded them of the Stuarts and France of the Bourbons. Princes "grant" such guarantees, but the force of things gives them. The returning Bourbons believed they had bestowed the charter and could take it back, that right divine was theirs and France possessed nothing. They looked glum at every development of the century and did not see that the hand which removed Napoleon had brought them in too. France had done without them for twenty-two years; the nation's roots were everywhere except under the throne.

Believing itself strong, the Restoration one morning contested the sovereignty of the nation and the liberty of the citizen in the ordinances of July, and fell, justly. Yet Hugo credits it: under Louis XVIII and Charles X, after the Revolution's word and Bonaparte's cannon, intelligence had its turn; for fifteen years equality before the law, liberty of conscience, speech and press were seen at work in peace. The Bourbons were an instrument of civilisation that broke in the hands of Providence. Their fall had grandeur on the nation's side rather than theirs: Charles X, sailing from Cherbourg, fussed over a round table being cut square. The people, attacked by a royal insurrection, defended itself, set the old king gently on the ground and halted, carrying away respect but not regret.

The Revolution of July had friends and enemies at once across Europe; the princes, owls of this dawn, shut their eyes and opened them only to threaten, offended that the revolution was formidable and yet gentle, shedding no royal blood. Hugo defines it as the triumph of right overthrowing fact, hence both its brilliance and its mildness. Right is the just and the true and remains eternally pure; fact, however necessary, becomes deformed and monstrous over time, as Machiavelli shows, who is simply the fact of the sixteenth century. To reconcile right and fact is the task of sages.

title: Badly Sewed
summary: The sages' task is one thing, the clever men's another: the "statesmen" of 1830 arrested the revolution halfway, manufactured a dynasty to cover the scaffolding, and found their man of "Halt" in Louis Philippe d'Orléans, crowned by the 221 deputies and Lafayette at the Hôtel de Ville.
details: As soon as a revolution has made the coast, Hugo says, the skilful hasten to prepare the shipwreck. The skilful of this century call themselves statesmen, a word that has become almost slang; where there is nothing but skill there is pettiness. They treat a revolution like a severed artery needing a prompt ligature: right proclaimed, now power must be strengthened. And after a revolution a people on a monarchical continent must, they say, procure itself a dynasty, which hides the scaffolding and covers the ambulance. A man of genius or of fortune can be made a king, Napoleon or Iturbide; but a dynasty needs the wrinkle of centuries, and must be national, revolutionary at a distance by ideas accepted rather than acts committed, historic and sympathetic. Royal houses are like Indian fig-trees whose branches root and become trees, on condition that they bend down to the people.

The great art is to make success sound like catastrophe, to muffle right, to wrap the giant people in flannel and put it to bed early, to dilute the event with the expedient. 1830 practised this theory, as 1688 had in England: a revolution stopped midway, half progress, quasi-right, and logic knows no "almost". Who stops revolutions halfway? The bourgeoisie, which Hugo defines not as a class but as the contented portion of the people, the man who now has time to sit down; a chair is not a caste. Its state after 1830 was not inertia but the halt, repose armed and on guard, the partition between 1830 and 1848.

The bourgeoisie and the statesmen needed a man who should express the word Halt, an Although-Because, signifying both revolution and stability. He was already found: Louis Philippe d'Orléans. The 221 made him king and Lafayette undertook the coronation, calling it "the best of republics"; the town hall of Paris replaced the cathedral of Rheims. This half-throne for a whole throne was "the work of 1830". When the skilful had finished, the vice of their solution appeared: all had been done outside absolute right, which cried "I protest!" and retired into the darkness.

title: Louis Philippe
summary: A long portrait of Louis Philippe: a rare man, careful, sober, brave and kindly, a king in broad daylight who fought the guillotine case by case, but modest in the name of France and too much a paternal king; Hugo separates what accuses royalty, the reign and the king, and testifies in the man's favour as one exile of another.
details: Revolutions, even debased like that of 1830, usually keep enough providential lucidity not to fall amiss, and 1830 had luck: the king amounted to more than royalty. Hugo piles up the traits of Louis Philippe in one immense sentence: son of a father more blamed than he deserved esteem; careful of his health, fortune and affairs; sober, serene, patient; a good man and a good prince; an admirable representative of the middle class and greater than it; a bourgeois from the day he became king; reputed but not proved a miser; a fascinating talker and an undeceived statesman, inwardly cold, governing at the shortest range, incapable of rancour and of gratitude; fond of his country but preferring his family; a general at Valmy and a soldier at Jemappes, attacked eight times by regicides and always smiling; a prodigious memory for deeds, names and dates but blind to tendencies and the hidden currents of souls; something of Charlemagne and something of an attorney. He would rank among history's most illustrious rulers had he loved glory a little, and had he felt what is great as keenly as what is useful.

He had been handsome and remained graceful, pleased the masses if not always the nation, wore no crown and no white hair, kept the old pronunciation and spelling in the service of modern opinions, went out with his umbrella under his arm, dabbled in masonry, gardening and medicine, and bled a fallen postilion. Hugo sorts the grievances into three columns: democratic right confiscated, progress made secondary, the street repressed, the Rue Transnonain and the councils of war belong to royalty; Belgium refused, Algeria too harshly conquered, Blaye, Deutz bought and Pritchard paid belong to the reign; a policy more domestic than national belongs to the king. His great fault was to be modest in the name of France, too much the paternal king incubating a dynasty and afraid of being disturbed, though his family deserved his tenderness.

Louis Philippe was 1830 made man, Prince Equality, carrying in himself the contradiction of Restoration and Revolution, and exile was his great recommendation to the throne: proscribed and poor, he had sold a horse for bread in Switzerland and taught mathematics at Reichenau while his sister Adelaide sewed. He had demolished the iron cage of Mont-Saint-Michel with his own hands, had been Dumouriez's companion and Lafayette's friend, had known Mirabeau and Danton, and at twenty-four had watched the trial of Louis XVI from a box, which left in him a respectful fear of the immense justices of the people. He could recite from memory the whole letter A of the Constituent Assembly's roll. He was a king of broad daylight: under him press, tribune, conscience and speech were free.

History has not yet pronounced on him; Louis Blanc has softened his first verdict. Elected by two "almosts", the 221 and 1830, he can be judged here only with reservations in the name of absolute democratic right, but taken in himself he will remain one of the best princes who ever sat on a throne. Take away the king and the man is good, at times admirable: after days of wrestling with the diplomacy of Europe he sat up at night revising death sentences, fighting the guillotine foot by foot against his crown attorneys ("I won seven last night"); in his early years the death penalty was as good as abolished, and after Fieschi's machine he regretted not being wounded so that he might pardon. Hugo closes by saying that a man who is himself a phantom today and knew that king may testify for him before history; an epitaph penned by a dead man is sincere, and one shade may console another.

title: Cracks Beneath the Foundation
summary: Hugo absolves both the king, who held power in good faith, and the democracy that attacked him, then surveys the pressures on the July monarchy: legitimists and republicans assailing it from both sides, armed peace abroad, the social questions and socialist thinkers at home, and the crises of early 1832 that made the year open with something impending.
details: Because the story is about to enter one of the tragic clouds at the beginning of Louis Philippe's reign, the narrator wants no equivocation about the king. He came to the throne without violence or personal initiative, born a prince and believing himself elected king, convinced, wrongly but sincerely, that the offer accorded with right and its acceptance with duty. Since both the king and the democracy acted in good faith, the terror of the social conflict weighs on neither: a clash of principles is like a clash of elements, and those in error are sincerely so; a blind man is no more a criminal than a Vendean is a ruffian. These collisions are to be imputed to the fatality of things.

The government of 1830 had to fight the day after it was born. God writes his will in events as an obscure text, and men make hasty translations of it: each translation a party, each misreading a faction. The old legitimist parties attacked the revolution in its royalty ("Revolution, why this king?"), illogically, since in such revolutions it is the king who revolts and not the people, revolution being the contrary of revolt; the republicans raised the same cry logically, because 1830 had bankrupted the people. Abroad, having become a monarchy, it had to keep the peace with Europe, hence armed peace; pushed on by progress in France, it pushed on the loitering monarchies. Within, pauperism, wages, education, prisons, prostitution, the fate of women, capital and labour multiplied above society like a terrible slope.

Outside the parties, thinkers, whom Hugo gathers under the name socialists, tranquilly mined into the volcano, raising the question of happiness rather than of rights and adding to the rights of man those of woman and child. Their problems reduce to two: to produce wealth and to share it, employment of forces and distribution of enjoyment, public power and individual happiness. England solves only the first and so breeds monstrous opulence beside monstrous wretchedness; communism and agrarian law think they solve the second and kill production, a partition made by the butcher. Both must be solved together: encourage the wealthy, protect the poor, suppress misery, adjust wages to labour, make education free and compulsory, make property universal rather than abolish it; then one is worthy to be called France. These doctrines, the need to reckon with philosophers, a new politics to be invented, the use of Lafayette to defend Polignac, all weighed on Louis Philippe, who felt under his feet a formidable disaggregation that was nevertheless not dust.

Twenty months after July, 1832 opened menacingly: distress and laborers without bread, the last Prince de Condé dead in the shadows, Belgium offering herself to a French prince and given to an English one, Nicolas's hatred, Ferdinand in Spain and Miguel in Portugal, Italy quaking, Poland nailed in her coffin, England a suspected ally, the peerage refusing four heads to the law, the fleurs-de-lys erased from the king's carriage and the cross torn from Notre-Dame, Lafayette lessened, Laffitte ruined, Benjamin Constant dead in indigence, Casimir Périer dead exhausted; civil war in Paris, servile war at Lyons; the Duchesse de Berry in the Vendée, plots, risings and cholera, adding the roar of events to the roar of ideas.

title: Facts Whence History Springs and Which History Ignores
summary: From police reports and found papers Hugo reconstructs the ferment of April 1832 in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine: oaths sworn in wine-shops, cartridges made all night, coded membership lists, caches of powder, the network of secret societies from the Society of the Rights of Man to the Friends of the A.B.C., and the faubourg itself as a powder-house of suffering and ideas.
details: By late April everything had come to the boil. Since 1830 small revolts had kept bursting out, signs of a vast conflagration beneath; France watched Paris and Paris watched the Faubourg Saint-Antoine. In the grave and stormy wine-shops of the Rue de Charonne workmen swore to take to the street at the first alarm; upstairs rooms held almost masonic initiations; "subversive" pamphlets were read aloud. Hugo quotes the talk: nobody knows the leaders and the day will be known only two hours before; three hundred men at ten sous each will buy powder and shot; one man does not sleep because he makes cartridges all night; "We have no arms!" "The soldiers have!" Well-dressed men came for ten minutes, shook hands with the most important and left. A man would drink and tell the wine-merchant the revolution would pay. A fencing master's trophy of foils one day lost its buttons.

The brewing became oddly notorious: women sweeping doorsteps spoke of cartridge-making; proclamations to the provincial National Guard were signed by a wine-merchant; a bearded man with an Italian accent read a manifesto from a stone post in the Marché Lenoir to applause. A man who shouted "I am a Babouvist!" and denounced the republicans was silenced as a police spy. A workman was warned near the canal by a stranger from "the committee" that an eye was fixed on him. Two ragged passers-by: "Who governs us?" "M. Philippe." "No, it is the bourgeoisie." A carpenter in the Rue de Reuilly found torn papers: a committee note about recruiting and a cache of five or six thousand guns, a list headed Q C D E (quinturions, centurions, decurions, éclaireurs) with names, arms and a coded date, April 15th 1832, and a third paper mixing the sections of the Society of the Rights of Man with Kosciusko, Washington, Hoche, Marseillaise and the sovereignty of the people. Searches turned up gray paper folded into cartridges with a powder recipe, a mason's package of printed dialogues and a tin of cartridges, children's finds of a bullet-mould and melted lead, a man caught at five in the morning making cartridges; two hundred thousand cartridges were distributed in the faubourg one week and thirty thousand the next, and the police seized none. Shopkeepers asked workmen how the rising was coming along as they would ask after a wife.

The network of societies spread like a membrane: from the Friends of the People sprang the Society of the Rights of Man, with sections named Pikes, Tocsin, Phrygian Cap, January 21, Robespierre, Ça Ira, which begot the Society of Action; alongside them the Gallic Society, societies for the press and against indirect taxes, the Equal Workingmen split into levellers, communists and reformers, and the Army of the Bastilles in which no more than five men knew one another. The Parisian societies had branches in Lyons, Nantes, Lille and Marseilles, each with its Cougourde. The schools stirred as much as the faubourgs: the Friends of the A.B.C., affiliated with the Mutualists of Angers and the Cougourde of Aix, met at the Café Musain and at the wine-shop Corinthe in the Rue Mondétour. The army too was mined, and liberty trees went up in Burgundy and the south.

Hugo closes on the Faubourg Saint-Antoine itself, laborious, angry as a hive, suffering under attic roofs and full of rare ardent minds, where misery and intelligence meet; a reservoir of people whose cabarets, like the taverns on the Sibyl's cave, intoxicate on words more than wine. In '93 it sent forth now savage legions, now heroic bands: savages, yes, but the savages of civilisation, demanding light with the mask of night, whom he prefers to the civilised men of barbarism who politely glorify the sword, the stake and the scaffold. But a third choice remains: neither despotism nor terrorism; progress with a gentle slope, which is God's whole policy.

title: Enjolras and His Lieutenants
summary: At a secret meeting in the Café Musain, Enjolras sends each of the Friends of the A.B.C. to sound a group of potential fighters across Paris. Grantaire begs to be trusted with the lukewarm workmen at the Barrière du Maine; when Enjolras looks in at Richefeu's later, he finds him deep in a game of dominoes.
details: About this time Enjolras, foreseeing a possible catastrophe, takes a kind of mysterious census. In the back room of the Café Musain he tells the friends they must know where they stand and whom they can count on, and that it must be done today: Courfeyrac to the polytechnic students on their day out, Feuilly to the men of the Glacière, Combeferre to Picpus, Bahorel to the Estrapade, Prouvaire to the masons' lodge in the Rue de Grenelle-Saint-Honoré, Joly to Dupuytren's clinical lecture to feel the pulse of the medical school, Bossuet to the young law licentiates in the courts; he will take the Cougourde himself. One important group remains: the marble-workers, painters and sculptors' journeymen at the Barrière du Maine, enthusiasts liable to cool, who have taken to playing dominoes at Richefeu's and need someone to talk to them with firmness. He had counted on "that abstracted Marius", who no longer comes.

Grantaire offers himself. Enjolras is incredulous: Grantaire, who believes in nothing, to warm cold hearts in the name of principle? "I believe in you," Grantaire answers. Told to sleep off his absinthe and not meddle, he protests that he is terrible when he sets about it, knows the Social Contract and the constitution of the Year Two by heart, keeps an old Republican bank-bill in his drawer, and can talk superb twaddle for six hours by the clock. Enjolras gravely consents to try him. Grantaire goes home and returns in five minutes wearing a red Robespierre waistcoat, lays his hand on its scarlet points, whispers "Be easy" in Enjolras's ear, and sets out.

A quarter of an hour later the back room is empty, each friend gone to his task. Walking towards the abandoned quarries at Issy where the Cougourde of Aix meets, Enjolras reviews the situation: the people are again taking possession of right, the furnace is being heated, and he has a powder train of friends laid across Paris, Combeferre's eloquence, Feuilly's enthusiasm, Courfeyrac's dash, Bahorel's smile, Prouvaire's melancholy, Joly's science, Bossuet's sarcasm. This makes him think of Grantaire, and since the Barrière du Maine is not far out of his way he decides to look in at Richefeu's.

One o'clock strikes from Vaugirard as he pushes open the smoky door and stands with folded arms. Through the haze he hears Grantaire's voice, hammering a marble table strewn with bran and dominoes and arguing with an adversary: double-six, fours, blank, domino, plague take it. Grantaire is playing dominoes.

title: The Lark’s Meadow
summary: Marius leaves the Gorbeau house the morning after the ambush and moves in with Courfeyrac, avoiding Javert and the coming trial; every Monday he sends five borrowed francs to Thénardier in La Force. Knowing less than ever about the girl, he drifts in idle reverie until a passer-by names a lonely field by the Gobelins river "the Lark's meadow", and he returns to it every day.
details: As soon as Javert has carried off his prisoners in three cabs, Marius slips out too and goes to sleep on a mattress on the floor at Courfeyrac's, who now lives in the Rue de la Verrerie "for political reasons". At seven next morning he returns, pays Ma'am Bougon the quarter's rent, loads his books, bed, table, commode and two chairs on a handcart and leaves no address, so that when Javert comes back to question him he hears only "Moved away!" Ma'am Bougon is convinced the girlish young man was in league with the robbers. Marius has two reasons: horror of the house where he saw the wicked poor man, a deformity perhaps worse than the wicked rich man, and an unwillingness to appear in the lawsuit and testify against Thénardier. Javert supposes the young lawyer, whose name he has forgotten, has taken fright, and does not find him.

Months pass. Learning from a law student that Thénardier is in close confinement, Marius has five francs handed in to the clerk's office of La Force for him every Monday; having no money, he borrows them from Courfeyrac, the first loan of his life, a riddle to the lender and to the receiver alike. Marius is heartbroken. He had seen the girl and the old man who seemed her father at close quarters, and a gust swept them away without one spark of certainty. She was not Ursule; the Lark is only a nickname; the old man, in hiding from the police, disguised as a workman near the Invalides, heroic and equivocal, may or may not be her father, may or may not be the man Thénardier recognised. His whole life is now absolute uncertainty within an impenetrable fog; he still longs to see her but no longer expects to.

Poverty returns. He had long since stopped working, and the narrator warns that reverie, wholesome as a narcotic in small doses, drowns when it replaces thought: the generous poor man who does not work is lost, and that slope ends in suicide or crime. Marius descends it slowly with his eyes on the girl he cannot see, feeling his coats, shirts, hat and boots wearing out and saying, "If I could but see her once again before I die!" One sweet thought remains, that she loved him and perhaps thinks of him still; at dusk he pours his purest reveries into a notebook, which he calls "writing to her". His reason is not deranged; stripped of hope, his judgment grows clearer than ever, and the soul that loves and suffers is in a state of sublimity.

Beyond the Rue de la Santé and the Glacière, near the little river of the Gobelins, lies a green meadow strung with drying linen, with an old market-gardener's house of Louis XIII's time, a little water among poplars, and the Panthéon, the Val-de-Grâce and the towers of Notre-Dame on the horizon, the one spot on the boulevards where Ruysdael would sit down, and therefore deserted. Marius's strolls lead him there. One day he asks a rare passer-by its name: "It is the Lark's meadow," where Ulbach killed the shepherdess of Ivry. After the word "Lark" Marius hears nothing more. It has replaced Ursule in his melancholy. "This is her meadow. I shall know where she lives now." Absurd, but irresistible: he returns to the meadow of the Lark every day.

title: Embryonic Formation of Crimes in the Incubation of Prisons
summary: Javert's triumph was incomplete: the victim escaped, Montparnasse got away after leading Éponine off her post, and Claquesous vanished on the way to La Force, perhaps with police connivance. In prison Brujon, left loose to make him talk, sends out coded messages and a note to Babet about "an affair in the Rue Plumet, a gate on a garden"; passed through Magnon to the newly released Éponine, it comes back marked "biscuit": nothing to be done.
details: Javert's victory in the Gorbeau hovel had its gaps.
