His chief anxiety was that he had not taken the prisoner: the assassinated man who flees is more suspicious than the assassin, and would have been a fine prize for the authorities. Montparnasse had escaped too, having met Éponine on watch under the trees and led her off, preferring to play the lover with the daughter rather than the brigand with the father. Éponine was later seized and joined Azelma at the Madelonettes. And between the Gorbeau house and La Force, Claquesous had been lost, melted out of the handcuffs and the cab like a snowflake in water. Was there connivance? Javert bristles at such compromises, but his squad includes inspectors more initiated than he, and Claquesous was villain enough to make a very good agent. Such double-edged rascals exist. As for the booby of a lawyer whose name he has forgotten, Javert cares little; a lawyer can be hunted up any time.

The magistrate leaves one of the Patron-Minette band, Brujon, the long-haired man of the Rue du Petit-Banquier, out of close confinement in the Charlemagne yard in the hope that he will chatter. A "Brujon, 1811" carved on a wall of the Lions' Ditch at La Force was his father's. This Brujon is a cunning young spark with a plaintive air who seems stupefied by prison, staring for hours at the sutler's price list and complaining of fever. Robbers, Hugo notes, do not interrupt their profession because they are in the hands of justice; they are artists with one picture in the salon and another on the easel. Late in February 1832 it comes out that he has paid the prison errand-men fifty sous for three commissions under comrades' names, to the Panthéon, the Val-de-Grâce and the Barrière de Grenelle, the homes of three redoubtable prowlers, Kruideniers alias Bizarro, Glorieux and Barre-Carosse, who are promptly arrested. A week later a watchman catches Brujon writing at night; he gets a month in solitary, but the paper is not found.

Next morning a "postilion", a pellet of bread with a note inside, is thrown from the Charlemagne yard over the five-storey building into the Lions' Ditch. It reaches Babet, one of the four heads of Patron-Minette, in solitary, and reads: "Babet. There is an affair in the Rue Plumet. A gate on a garden." Babet passes it to a woman friend in the Salpêtrière, who passes it to Magnon, a woman suspected by the police but not yet arrested, who has relations with the Thénardiers (to be described later) and can bridge the Salpêtrière and the Madelonettes. Just then, for lack of proof against them, Éponine and Azelma are released, and Magnon, waiting at the gate, gives Éponine the note and tells her to look into it. Éponine goes to the Rue Plumet, finds the gate and garden, watches the house for days, and brings Magnon back a biscuit, which in prison symbolism means: nothing to be done. When Brujon and Babet cross in the prison yard, "Well? the Rue P.?" "Biscuit." So Brujon's crime miscarried, though, the narrator adds, the miscarriage had consequences of its own, quite distinct from his programme: when we think we are knotting one thread we are often tying another.

title: Apparition to Father Mabeuf
summary: Old M. Mabeuf, sunk in poverty and his indigo experiments, cannot even draw water for his drooping garden one dry evening when a tall ragged girl springs from the hedge, waters every bed, and asks in return only where M. Marius lives. He sends her to the Lark's meadow and, when she vanishes, half believes she was a goblin.
details: Marius sees no one now, but sometimes meets Father Mabeuf by chance; both are descending the cellar stairs of misery. The Flora of Cauteretz no longer sells at all; the indigo trials in the shady garden at Austerlitz have failed, and Mabeuf has pawned his copper plates to get a sunny corner in the Jardin des Plantes to try again at his own expense. He breakfasts on two eggs and leaves one for his old servant, unpaid for fifteen months; often that is his only meal. Grown morose, he no longer receives visitors, and when the old man and the young one pass on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital they only exchange a melancholy nod; misery has loosened their bond. Royol the bookseller is dead. Mabeuf, nearly eighty, dreams that his balls of blueing will make him rich enough to redeem his plates and buy a 1655 Art de Naviguer.

One evening, with Mother Plutarque ill in bed, he dines on a bone and a crust and sits on an overturned stone post in his garden reading two books on demons and on the goblins of the Bièvre, which interest him because his garden was once haunted. Four rainless days have left his beloved rhododendron drooping. He rises to draw water but has not even the strength to unhook the well-chain, and looks up at a sky filling with stars: not a cloud, not a drop. "A tear of dew! A little pity!" He tries the chain again and fails.

A voice asks, "Father Mabeuf, would you like to have me water your garden for you?" Something like a wild animal passes through the hedge and a tall, slender girl, barefoot in a tattered petticoat, stands boldly before him, a form blossomed out of the twilight. Before the timid old man can speak she has unhooked the chain, filled the watering-pot, and is running among the beds distributing life, black and angular as a bat. She draws bucket after bucket and waters the whole garden. Mabeuf, in tears, lays his hand on her brow and calls her an angel who takes care of flowers. "No, I am the devil, but that's all the same to me," she says. He laments that he is too poor to do anything for her. "You can do something. Tell me where M. Marius lives."

He searches his memory: Monsieur Marius, the Baron Marius Pontmercy. He lived, or rather no longer lives, he does not know where; then, bending to train a branch, he recalls that Marius often passes along the boulevard towards the Glacière and the Rue Croulebarbe, to the Lark's meadow; it is not hard to meet him there. When he straightens up the girl is gone. Decidedly terrified, he reflects that if his garden had not been watered he would take her for a spirit, and falling asleep an hour later wonders whether, as Rubaudière describes, it could have been a goblin.

title: An Apparition to Marius
summary: Some days later Éponine, out of prison and poorer and prettier than before, finds Marius at the Lark's meadow: she has the young lady's address and will take him there. Marius makes her swear not to give it to her father, and in his joy does not see her grief; when he offers her the five francs meant for Thénardier, she lets the coin fall: "I don't want your money."
details: One Monday morning, the day he borrows a hundred-sou piece from Courfeyrac for Thénardier, Marius takes a stroll before carrying it to the prison, hoping it will help him work on his return; it never does. He is supposed to be translating the Gans and Savigny controversy, reads four lines, sees a star between himself and the paper, and goes out to the Lark's meadow, where he sees the star more than ever. He lives there more than at Courfeyrac's; his real address is the seventh tree from the Rue Croulebarbe on the Boulevard de la Santé. That morning he sits on the parapet of the Gobelins river in the spring sun, dreaming of "Her" and reproaching himself for his paralysis of soul, hearing the laundresses beating linen below and birds in the elms above, the sound of toil and the sound of liberty.

A familiar voice says, "Come! Here he is!" It is the wretched girl who came to his room one morning, the elder of the Thénardier daughters, Éponine; he knows her name now. She has grown poorer and prettier at once, barefoot and in rags two months older, with straw in her hair from sleeping in a stable loft and the terrified, lamentable look that prison adds to wretchedness, and in spite of it all she is beautiful. She has hunted for him for six weeks: she was in the jug a fortnight and released since there was nothing against her and she is two months short of the age of discretion; Father Mabeuf was right that he could be found on this boulevard. He has moved, she understands, because of "that affair". She chatters about his old hat, the hole in his shirt she must mend, and Mabeuf calling him Baron; Marius barely answers. "You don't seem glad to see me." He is silent. Then: if she chooses, she can force him to look glad. He asks what she means. "Ah! you used to call me thou." "Well, then, what dost thou mean?"

She hesitates, struggling, then decides: so much the worse. She wants him to smile, and reminds him he promised to give her anything she liked. "I have the address." Marius turns pale. The address he asked her to get, "of that young lady", she says, and sighs deeply. He leaps from the parapet and seizes her hand: lead him there, ask anything. She does not know the street or number well but knows the house, in quite another direction; she will take him. "Oh! how glad you are!" she says in a tone that would have rent any observer's heart but does not graze his.

A cloud crosses his brow. He grips her arm: swear not to give this address to her father. She stares, stupefied: how does he know that her name is Éponine? "That's nice! You have called me Éponine!" She does not seem to hear his demand until he shakes her, then laughs: her father is in close confinement, and what does she care for him; yes, she swears, she will not tell him, nor anyone. They set off at once, she walking ahead so that a nice young man will not be seen with "a woman like me", a word no tongue can express in that child's mouth. After a dozen paces she reminds him sideways that he promised her something. All he owns is the five francs intended for Thénardier the father; he lays them in her hand. She opens her fingers, lets the coin fall to the ground, and looks at him gloomily: "I don't want your money."
